title: A watermark closes a window; a late event misses it

steps.say: A source sends events with their own event time. First: e1 with time 10:01. The operator keeps it in the 10:00-10:05 window.
e2 arrives with time 10:04. It also belongs to the same window, so the buffer holds two events.
The watermark says: no event older than this time is expected. Rule: watermark = newest event time minus 2 minutes of allowed delay.
e3 arrives with time 10:07. The newest time is now 10:07, so the watermark moves to 10:05.
Watermark 10:05 has reached the window end 10:05. The window closes and sends its result: count = 2.
Failure: e4 with time 10:03 was delayed on the network and shows up now. Its time is below the watermark 10:05, so it is late.
The window already sent its answer, so e4 is not counted. Result 2 is now wrong; the real count is 3.
Fix 1: send late events to a side output, so they can be fixed later or counted in a correction.
Fix 2: wait longer. A 5-minute delay would catch e4, but then the result for 10:05 is sent at 10:10 instead. More waiting means more correct but slower.

title: Tumbling and sliding windows

steps.say: Tumbling windows cut time into fixed 5-minute pieces with no overlap. Every event goes into exactly one piece.
Event at 10:02 lands in window 10:00-10:05.
Event at 10:04 lands in the same window.
Event at 10:06 belongs to the next piece, 10:05-10:10. Window 1 is now final: 2 clicks per 5 minutes.
Now the sliding window: size 10 minutes, slide 5 minutes. A new window starts every 5 minutes, so windows overlap.
The 10:06 event is inside both 10:00-10:10 and 10:05-10:15. One event is counted twice, once per window.
The 10:02 and 10:04 events are only in the first sliding window, so it holds 3 events: a smooth 10-minute count updated every 5 minutes.
Cost: each event is stored in size/slide = 2 windows. A 1-hour window sliding every 1 minute would copy every event 60 times.

title: Session windows and a late event that merges two sessions

steps.say: A session window has no fixed size. It stays open while events keep coming, and closes after a 30-second gap with no events.
Click at 0 s opens session A. It will close at 0+30 = 30 s unless more clicks arrive.
Click at 10 s and click at 25 s each push the end later. Session A now runs until 25+30 = 55 s with 3 clicks.
Nothing arrives for 30 s, so at 55 s session A closes and sends its result.
Click at 100 s starts a new session B. It would run 100 s to 130 s.
Failure case: a late click with time 80 s arrives. It is 25 s after the end of A, which is less than the 30 s gap.
A now ends at 80+30 = 110 s, which overlaps B (starts 100 s). The two sessions merge into one.
The earlier result A=3 is now wrong. The engine must send a correction: one session with 5 clicks.

title: A checkpoint barrier, a crash, and a restore

steps.say: A stream job reads a log and counts events. Every few seconds the coordinator starts a checkpoint: a saved copy of all state.
The source writes a special barrier into the stream, and saves its own position: offset 1000.
The barrier travels with the data. When the counter sees it, all events before the barrier are counted, so it saves count = 1000.
The sink sees the barrier and tells the coordinator. All parts saved, so checkpoint 7 is complete.
Work continues. The job reads offsets 1000 to 1450 and counts up to 1450. These 450 events are not in any checkpoint yet.
Failure: the counter machine crashes. Its memory is gone, including count 1450.
The job restarts and loads checkpoint 7 from the store: counter back to 1000.
The source also rewinds to the saved offset 1000, so the same 450 events are read again.
The counter replays offsets 1000 to 1450 and reaches 1450 again. Each event counted exactly once in state, even though it was read twice.

title: A slow stage pushes back up the pipeline

steps.say: A pipeline: Kafka, Parse, Enrich, Sink. Each stage has a small buffer of 32 records. Everything runs at 1000 records per second.
Enrich calls a slow service and drops to 200 records per second. It takes 200 in but Parse still sends 1000.
5 seconds later the buffer in front of Enrich is full: 32/32. Enrich has no room to accept more.
Parse cannot hand over its output, so its own buffer fills: 32/32. Parse now blocks and stops reading.
This is backpressure: the slowness travels backward. Parse reads Kafka only at 200 per second now, matching Enrich.
The records wait safely in Kafka, which is on disk. Lag grows by 800 per second, 4800 after 6 s. Memory in the job stays flat.
Without backpressure, Parse would keep pushing 800 extra records per second into memory. After a few minutes the job would crash with out-of-memory.
The team scales Enrich from 1 to 5 workers: 1000 per second again. Buffers drain and the chain speeds up.
Enrich now handles 1000 per second plus a catch-up burst, so the 4800 lagging records are cleared in about 30 s and lag returns to 0.

title: A consumer crashes and the group rebalances

steps.say: Topic orders has 4 partitions. Group billing has 2 consumers. Each partition goes to exactly one consumer: C1 gets P0 and P1, C2 gets P2 and P3.
Consumers commit their position now and then. C1 commits P0=520, C2 commits P2=480.
C2 keeps working and reads P2 up to offset 520, but its next commit is not due yet. All the time it sends heartbeats.
Failure: C2 crashes. The heartbeats stop.
After the 10 s session timeout the coordinator decides C2 is dead and starts a rebalance. Everyone pauses reading.
New plan: C1 takes all 4 partitions. P2 and P3 move from C2 to C1.
C1 starts P2 from the last committed offset 480, not 520. The 40 messages (481 to 520) are processed twice, so handlers should be safe to repeat.
A new consumer C3 starts and joins the group. Another rebalance runs.
The new plan: C1 keeps P0 and P1, C3 takes P2 and P3. Load is even again. A fifth consumer would get nothing, because 4 partitions allow at most 4 active consumers.

title: Compaction keeps the newest value for each key

steps.say: A topic holds the latest profile per key. Six records so far: A was written 3 times, B twice, C once. Offsets never change.
The cleaner scans the log. For key A it finds A=3 at offset 5 is the newest. For key B, B=2 at offset 4 is the newest.
Old values are removed: off0, off1 and off2. Kept: off3, off4, off5. The offsets keep their numbers, so there are gaps.
A new reader starting at offset 0 sees C=1, B=2, A=3. That is the full latest state, just smaller than the full history.
To delete key A, a producer writes a tombstone: A=null at offset 6. A tombstone is a normal record with an empty value.
Next compaction removes A=3 because A=null is newer. The tombstone itself stays, so readers learn A was deleted.
After delete.retention.ms (default 24 hours) the tombstone is removed too. Key A is now gone from the log.
Failure case: a consumer was offline for 2 days. It never saw A=null, and the tombstone is gone. It still has A=3 in its own database.
Rule: keep tombstones longer than the slowest consumer can be offline. Otherwise some copies of deleted data live on.

title: Lost message, lost ack and a duplicate

steps.say: At-most-once: the producer sends m1 and never retries. The network drops it.
The broker log is empty, and nobody knows. m1 is lost forever. Fast and simple, but data can disappear.
At-least-once: the producer sends m2 and waits for an ack. The broker stores it at offset 5.
The broker's ack is lost on the way back. The producer cannot tell if m2 was stored or not.
After 5 seconds the producer retries m2, because losing data is worse than sending it twice.
The log now has m2 twice, at offsets 5 and 6. A consumer will see a duplicate.
Exactly-once writes: the producer has PID=7 and numbers its messages. m3 is sent with seq=0 and stored at offset 7.
The ack is lost again and the producer retries m3 with the same seq=0. The broker sees it already stored seq=0 from PID=7, ignores the copy, and just acks.

The consumer side must also be safe: it reads m3, writes the result, and crashes before committing offset 7. It would read m3 again. Fix: save the result and the offset in one transaction, or make the handler idempotent.

title: Cache-aside, then a stampede when a hot key expires

steps.say: A client asks the app for user:42. The app checks the cache first.
Cache miss. The app asks the database. The query takes 20 ms.
The app puts the row in the cache with TTL = 60 seconds, and answers the client.
Next requests are cache hits: about 1 ms, and the database sees nothing. With 98% hits, 1000 req/s become only 20 req/s on the database.
At 60 seconds the TTL runs out and user:42 disappears from the cache. This is a very popular key.
Failure: in the next 20 ms, about 20 requests all miss the cache and all query the database for the same row. For a key with 1000 req/s and a slow query, this becomes hundreds.
The database slows from 20 ms to 2 s. More requests pile up while waiting, so even more miss. This chain is the stampede.
Fix 1: single-flight. The first miss takes a lock and loads the row. The other 999 wait about 20 ms and then read the new cache entry. The database gets 1 query.
Fix 2: add random jitter to TTL, for example 60 s plus or minus 10 s, so thousands of keys written together do not all expire in the same second.

title: LRU evicts the oldest-used key; a scan pushes out hot keys

steps.say: An LRU cache with room for 3 keys. Top slot = used most recently, bottom slot = used longest ago. Request: GET A.
GET B. B goes on top and A moves down one slot.
GET C. The cache is now full: C, B, A.
GET A again is a hit. A moves to the top, so now the oldest is B.
GET D is a miss and the cache is full. LRU removes the least recently used key: B.
Failure: a nightly job scans 1000 keys once (X1 to X1000). Each new key pushes out the oldest one, so A, C and D are all gone after 3 scans.
Morning traffic asks for A again: miss. The scan keys are never used again, but they took the space. This is cache pollution.
LFU counts uses instead of recency. A has 50 hits, scan keys only 1 hit each, so the scan keys are evicted first and A stays.

title: A CDN edge: miss, hit, stale file and purge

steps.say: A user asks for /logo.png. The request goes to the nearest edge server in Mumbai, not to the origin.
The edge has no copy, so it goes to the origin in the US. Round trip is about 180 ms.
The origin answers with the file (200 KB) and a header: Cache-Control: max-age=3600. That means: keep it for 1 hour.
The edge sends it to the user. This first user waited 190 ms.
A second user in Mumbai asks for the same file. Edge hit: 12 ms, and the origin does not see this request.
Failure: the team uploads a new logo, v2. The edge still has v1 with 3100 s left, so users keep seeing the old logo for up to 52 minutes.
Fix: send a purge request for /logo.png. The edge deletes its copy. Better: put a version in the name, like logo.v2.png, so no purge is needed.
Next request is a miss, so the edge fetches v2 and caches it again with a fresh 3600 s.
When max-age ends, the edge asks the origin: 'If-None-Match: abc'. If the file is unchanged, origin replies 304 with no body, so almost nothing is downloaded.

title: Round robin, a failed server, and least connections

steps.say: Request 1 comes in. Round robin sends requests to the servers in turn: first S1.
Request 2 goes to S2.
Request 3 goes to S3, then request 4 goes back to S1. Each server gets one third.
Failure: S2 crashes. The balancer checks GET /health on each server every 5 s. S2 does not answer.
Until it is marked down, requests still go to S2 and fail. Request 5 gets an error.
After 3 failed checks (15 s), the balancer removes S2 from the list. The arrow disappears.
Requests 6, 7 and 8 now alternate between S1 and S3. Users see no more errors, but each server takes 50% instead of 33%.
S2 is repaired. After 2 checks in a row pass, the balancer puts it back.
Round robin ignores load. If S1 has a slow request type with 50 open connections and S3 has 5, 'least connections' sends the next request to S3.

title: A token bucket allows a burst, then blocks

steps.say: Rule: a bucket holds up to 10 tokens and gets 5 new tokens every second. Each request takes 1 token. The bucket starts full.
Burst: 10 requests arrive in the same instant. Each takes a token, so all 10 pass. The bucket is empty.
Request number 11 arrives at once. No token left, so it is rejected with 429 Too Many Requests and 'Retry-After: 1'.
One second later, 5 tokens are added (5 per second).
The client retries and sends 5 requests. All 5 pass, and the bucket is empty again. Long-run speed can never be above 5 per second.
The client stays quiet for 2 seconds: +10 tokens, but the cap is 10. Idle time builds only a limited burst, never more.
Failure: with two API servers, each keeps its own counter. A user sending 10 requests to each gets 20 through, double the limit.
Fix: both limiters take tokens from one shared counter in Redis, using an atomic step. Now the user gets 10 in total across all servers.

title: TCP: handshake, data, a lost segment and a retransmit

steps.say: Before any data, TCP sets up a connection. The client picks a random start number and sends SYN seq=1000.
The server picks its own start number 5000 and answers SYN-ACK: seq=5000, ack=1001 (it expects client byte 1001 next).
The client confirms with ACK ack=5001. Both sides now agree on numbers, and the connection is open after 1 round trip.
The client sends 100 bytes of data: seq=1001, len=100. Every byte has a number, so the server can put them in order.
The server replies ACK ack=1101: 'I have everything before byte 1101, send 1101 next'.
Failure: the client sends seq=1101 len=100, but a router drops it. The client starts a retransmit timer (RTO = 200 ms).
The client keeps going. seq=1201 arrives, but the server still misses 1101, so it repeats ACK ack=1101. That is a duplicate ACK; 3 of them mean a hole.
The client resends seq=1101 (after the timer or 3 duplicate ACKs).
Now the server has 1101 to 1300 without a gap, and answers ACK ack=1301. Data is delivered in order, nothing missing.
To close, the client sends FIN seq=1301 and the server answers with ACK 1302. The server then sends its own FIN, so each direction closes by itself.

title: Slow start, congestion avoidance, and a loss that resets everything

steps.say: A sender does not know how fast the network is, so it starts small. cwnd (packets allowed in flight) = 1, slow-start limit ssthresh = 16.
The ACK comes back. In slow start every ACK adds 1, so cwnd doubles each round trip: next round 2 packets.
Next round cwnd = 4, then 8. Growth is fast: from 1 to 8 in just 3 round trips.
At cwnd = 16 it reaches ssthresh. Now it grows slowly: +1 packet per round trip (congestion avoidance). Next round is 17 packets.
17 packets arrive in a burst and the router queue (limit 8) overflows. Packets are dropped.
The sender gets no ACKs for the lost packets and its timer fires after 1 s. A timeout is a strong sign of congestion.
Reaction: ssthresh = half of cwnd = 8, and cwnd drops back to 1. All the speed is lost in one step.
Slow start again: 1, 2, 4, 8. It takes 3 round trips to be back to 8 packets, the old half-speed.
After 8 it climbs +1 per round trip: 9, 10, 11... Getting back to 17 takes 9 more round trips. Loss is expensive, and the sender repeats this saw-tooth shape.
Gentler case: if only one packet is lost and 3 duplicate ACKs arrive, the sender does fast retransmit and halves cwnd (17 to 8), skipping the reset to 1.

title: A TLS 1.3 handshake and a certificate failure

steps.say: The browser sends ClientHello: the ciphers it supports, its key_share (a public number for key exchange), and SNI=shop.com (the site name).
The server picks cipher TLS_AES_128_GCM and sends its own key_share in ServerHello. Both sides now compute the same secret key, never sent on the wire.
From here everything is encrypted. The server sends its certificate (its public key, name shop.com, signed by a CA) and a signature proving it owns the private key.
The browser checks three things: the name matches shop.com, today is inside the validity dates, and the signature chain leads to a trusted root CA.
The browser sends Finished. The handshake took 1 round trip. Now the HTTP request can go out.
Application data is encrypted with the shared key: GET /account. Anyone on the network sees only random-looking bytes.
Failure: on another visit the server's certificate expired on 2026-09-01. The check at step 4 fails.
The browser sends a fatal alert, closes the connection, and shows a warning page. No data is sent. A fake server cannot pass either: without shop.com's private key it cannot make the signature.

title: Resolving www.shop.com, caching, and a stale answer

steps.say: The browser asks the resolver: what is the IP of www.shop.com? The resolver cache is empty.
The resolver asks a root server. The root does not know the IP, but says: ask the .com servers.
The .com server also does not know the IP, but it knows who runs shop.com: ns1.shop.com.
The authority server for shop.com gives the real answer: A record 93.184.216.34, TTL 300 seconds.
The resolver stores the answer for 300 s and replies to the browser. This first lookup took about 120 ms with 3 round trips.
100 s later another user asks the same resolver. It answers from cache in 1 ms with 200 s left. No other server is asked.
Failure: shop.com moves to a new server and the authority now says 198.51.100.8.
Resolvers still hold the old answer, so they keep sending users to the old IP 93.184.216.34 until the TTL ends. Some users get the new site, some the old one.
At 300 s the cache entry expires. The next query goes to the authority and gets the new IP. Tip: lower TTL to 60 s a day before a move.

title: HTTP/1.1 waits in line; HTTP/2 shares one connection

steps.say: The browser has the page and needs 3 images: a.png (500 KB), b.png (5 KB), c.png (5 KB). It sends GET /a.png on one HTTP/1.1 connection.
The big image takes 400 ms. In HTTP/1.1 the next request waits for the response to finish, so b.png and c.png queue behind it.
Only then GET /b.png, 20 ms, and GET /c.png, 20 ms. Total about 440 ms; the small files waited for the big one (head-of-line blocking).
Old fix: open 6 parallel connections per site. It works, but each connection needs its own TCP and TLS handshake and memory.
HTTP/2 sends all three requests at the same time on one connection, as streams 1, 3 and 5.
The server splits responses into small frames and mixes them. b and c finish in 30 ms while a.png keeps streaming. Page is complete at 400 ms and small files were fast.

cl.sub: b, c at 30 ms; a at 400

steps.say: Failure: below HTTP/2 is one TCP stream. One packet carrying a piece of stream 1 is lost.
TCP must give bytes in order, so it holds all later data, even the finished frames of streams 3 and 5, until the retransmit arrives (about 1 round trip, 100 ms). All streams freeze together.
This blocking at the TCP level cannot be fixed inside HTTP/2. HTTP/3 solves it by using QUIC, where each stream recovers by itself.

title: QUIC: one-RTT start, loss on one stream, and a network change

steps.say: QUIC runs over UDP port 443. The client sends an Initial packet #0 that carries the TLS ClientHello inside it.
The server answers with its Initial and Handshake packets: ServerHello, certificate, Finished. Both keys are ready after one round trip.
The client can send the request right away. TCP + TLS would need 2 round trips before this; QUIC needs 1. HTTP request goes on stream 4.
The server answers with three packets: #5 carries stream 4 (the HTML), #6 carries stream 8 (app.js), #7 carries more of stream 4. Packet #5 is lost.
Stream 8 is complete and goes to the app right now. Stream 4 waits for its missing bytes, but nothing else is blocked. (In TCP, everything would wait.)
The client sends an ACK that says: I have #6 and #7, but not #5.
The server resends the same stream-4 bytes, but in a new packet #8. Packet numbers are never reused, so there is no confusion about which copy was acknowledged.
Network change: the phone leaves Wi-Fi and moves to 5G. Its IP changes from 10.0.0.5 to 100.64.2.9. A TCP connection would break here, because it is tied to the IP addresses.
QUIC packets carry the Connection ID 0xA1B2. The server sees the same ID from the new address, checks the new path, and continues. No new handshake, the download keeps going.

title: Routers pick the longest prefix; TTL stops a loop

steps.say: Host A sends a packet to 203.0.113.9 with TTL 64. It is not in A's own network, so A gives it to the default gateway R1.
R1 looks in its table: the only match is the default route 0.0.0.0/0, next hop R2. It lowers TTL by 1 and forwards.
R2 has two matching routes: 203.0.0.0/16 to R3 and 203.0.113.0/24 to R4. The router picks the longest prefix, the most specific: /24 to R4.
R4 is directly connected to the 203.0.113.0/24 network, so it delivers to Host B with TTL 61. Success.
Failure: a packet for 203.0.50.7 comes in. R2 matches only 203.0.0.0/16, so it sends the packet to R3.
R3 has a wrong route: 203.0.0.0/8 back to R2. The packet goes back and forth R2 to R3 to R2... TTL falls by 1 each hop.
After about 60 hops TTL reaches 0. The router that makes it 0 drops the packet and sends back an ICMP 'Time Exceeded' message to A.
Without TTL, looping packets would stay forever and fill the links. With TTL, the damage is limited and the error tells the admin where to look (traceroute uses this).

title: NAT rewrites addresses and forgets idle connections

steps.say: The PC has a private address that cannot be routed on the internet. It sends a packet from 192.168.1.10:51000 to the server 198.51.100.7:443.
The NAT router rewrites the source to its public address and a free port: 203.0.113.5:40001. It writes the pair into its table.
The phone also uses local port 51000. If the NAT only changed the IP, the two would clash. It gives the phone public port 40002.
The server answers to 203.0.113.5:40001. The NAT looks up 40001 in its table, rewrites the destination to 192.168.1.10:51000 and forwards.
A reply to port 40002 goes to the phone in the same way. One public IP can serve many devices, because the port tells them apart.
Failure: a stranger sends a packet to 203.0.113.5:40003. There is no table entry, so the NAT does not know which device it is for and drops it. That also works like a basic firewall.
Mappings expire. The phone's call has been silent for 120 s, so the NAT deletes its entry for port 40002.
Now the server sends audio to :40002. There is no entry any more, so the packet is dropped and the call goes silent. Fix: keep-alive packets every 25 s refresh the mapping.
